entries.text: Then nearly everything I do is a hobby, and fishing hungry is both. I don't have people. I have two owls who don't know me, and a smoke across the water that gets up later than I do.

entries.text: First page with the new pen, and it draws a thinner line. Wrote 'hobby: a labor you like' and 'work: one you have to do', and under it 'fishing: both'. Left a space at the bottom for people.

entries.text: Raked the ash open and the coals under it were still red from the morning; the twigs caught at once. While they did, tink, tink, tink came over the water, metal on metal, slow, a stop, then again. It has never come that clear.

entries.reason: He wanted, for once, to see who was making the sound instead of guessing.
entries.text: Every other time I went for a worm instead. Today is the day I said was off, and I left a space at the bottom of the page, so I walked down to the flat stone at the end of the stepping stones and stood there.

entries.text: On the open ground past the water someone stood at a plank table with a hammer: a little bigger than me, hair up in spikes, bare arms, and two round brass glasses over his eyes that caught the sun. He looked up, right at me. I didn't duck, and he didn't move either.
entries.title: He looked up

entries.reason: Token keeps to his own bank; the other one is bigger, and it's his place.
entries.text: He set the hammer down softly and bent back to his work, then went to a fire of his own in front of a cloth roof and lifted a tin off its stones. The stepping stones go all the way over. It is his ground over there, and I am small, so I came back to mine.
entries.title: Stayed on my side

entries.text: They're called goggles, and they keep things out of the eyes: chips and dust for people who cut wood, sparks and hard light for people who work metal with fire, wind for people who fly. He was hammering, so that fits. I don't know what he'd want with the last kind.

entries.text: Roasted a stickful of bindle acorns over the twigs' coals. If I lean out past the end of the ring I can see the stepping stones from here. I kept leaning.

entries.text: Ate the stickful on the log seat, blowing on each one first. Sun on my shell and the fire on my front; I could sit here all afternoon.

entries.text: Leaning out past the ring, I saw him crouched in the shallows on his side of the stepping stones, picking up flat stones. entries.text: Hello or goodbye, and it can't be both. He hasn't gone anywhere, so I think it was hello. I still don't know what I would have done with my stick.

entries.text: Knelt at the pool with the sun behind me, so my shadow fell on the bank and not the water. Across the water he was bent over his plank table, shaving at something, and looked up once.

entries.text: Sat on the flat stone at the end of the stepping stones to see. He has a long square stick on his table, pale as new wood, and he's sawing across it near the end, down to the middle and no farther. There are more like it stacked behind him.

entries.text: He stopped sawing and looked up, and I lifted my free hand, the one without the staff, and held it a breath like he did. He lifted his back, the empty one, the saw still in the other. Then we both put them down.

entries.text: Nothing else happened. He went back to sawing, slower than before, and I sat on the stone a while longer in the sun. It was enough.

entries.text: So he's making corners. A whole stack of square sticks is a lot of corners. He means to stay, I think.
